well, it really depends what you are trying to do with it. The thing to consider is that whatever velocity you achieve, you have to dump that much in to slow it down when you get to your destination.

For example, on a trip to Mars, you would use chemical rockets to get into a parking orbit around the earth. Once you are set to go, you would most likely use another chemical rocket to boost the delta-v up to and escape velocity, then switch to something like Ion propulsion, or maybe even nuclear propulsion.

Roughly calculating, for low earth orbit, you need to be travelling 7800 meters/second. To reach escape velocity from earth you need about 11200 meters/second, so you would need to add 3400 m/s delta-v.

I'm too lazy to find actual calculations about martian orbits, but its about half the size of earth, so lets assume, to maintain an orbit around Mars you need to be travelling about 4000 m/s. This means if you aren't using other means so slow down like atmospheric braking, you will need to add about 7200 m/s delta v retrograde (in the opposite direction of your velocity). An ion engine will take a lot longer to do that than a chemical rocket, but a chemical rocket will also be reducing mass a lot faster.

So in short it isn't really about how fast you can go, its how much delta V you can carry with you. A chemical rocket will give you some delta V very quickly, whereas an ion engine will give you massive amounts of delta V over time. If you burn an ion engine for a year straight on a low mass vessel, it will be hauling ass.

We have a few realistic options and multiple unrealistic option - conventional chemical engines, which brought men to the moon, solar sails, which are still in experimental phases, and ion engines. Chemical engines have a huge disadvantage, and that's that they require huge amounts of fuel, especially if you have a spacecraft that needs to last long and change directions. For example, the Saturn V carried something like 3,000 tons of fuel just to get about a 100 ton payload out of Earth orbit. Additionally, the lunar lander had to carry lots of fuel and even leave part of its landing system behind on the moon, just to get the astronauts back to the command module. Solar sails are large sheets that absorb photons and are propelled forward when struck. They have incredibly slow acceleration and need huge amounts of surface area to propel even small craft through space. There's ideas that they could potentially be powered be a laser shining from Earth. Although their acceleration is slow, they can accumulate speed over time and theoretically achieve high speeds. Ion engines are pretty damn cool, in my opinion. They use xenon gas for fuel and like the solar sail, have very slow acceleration, but can eventually reach (theoretical)speeds of 90,000 meters per second, according to NASA. This would make them well suited for transporting humans through space, as there would be no heavy G forces to deal with, unlike during the burn of a chemical engine, and they require very little fuel. For example, the Deep Space 1 probe reached 4,300 meters per second using only 74 kilos of xenon.
